But in multi-user collaboration with Agent editing, chronological order is not the same as the order in which the user wants to undo. The example in the article is highly representative: user A triggers the AI to rewrite paragraphs 2-3 while a human user adds a sentence to paragraph 4; when A clicks "undo AI changes", a global undo would innocently remove what the human just added—absolutely unacceptable in a collaborative document. The solution is to split rollback semantics into two types by identity boundary and enforce a design principle: the rollback boundary must equal the diff-comparison boundary. In implementation, the AI edit entry first "extracts" its own transaction from normal editing history and writes the boundary info; after the transaction reaches the Yjs side, UndoManager filters using the same metadata. u1qxet:339: The differences among Independent Peer, Attached Cursor, and Simulated User appear to be integration methods, but in essence they draw a traceable ownership boundary for "who changed what"—this boundary determines whether downstream diff comparison and undo/rollback can hold up. Independent Peer has the clearest ownership and naturally independent undo, at the cost of occupying collaborative seats and raising permission and sync complexity. Simulated User has the lowest integration cost but completely destroys trust, as users cannot distinguish their own changes from AI changes. Attached Cursor is the smoothest in permissions and experience, but without markers, the undo streams of AI and humans get mixed. The author's trade-off is not a choice among three, but an addition on the intermediate state: let Agent share the current user's context and permissions with an attached identity, yet stamp each round of editing with an independent "identity proof" (session ID/run round/message batch). The essence is both "not creating a virtual colleague" and "not fully disguising as a user", settling the ownership boundary into metadata that downstream mechanisms can consume.
